questions.explanation: Self-reported model confidence is not reliably calibrated for domain-specific tasks like legal classification — the model can express high certainty while being wrong, which means an escalation trigger built solely on that self-report is trivially bypassed by the model's own tendency toward assertiveness, exactly matching the observed symptom of near-zero escalation despite genuine ambiguity. The trap is option C, framing the gap as a definitional mismatch between the agent's and reviewers' standards of ambiguity — this is a real thing worth checking, but it doesn't explain a systematic pattern of the agent never escalating regardless of case difficulty; a definitional mismatch would produce some escalations at a different threshold, not near-total non-escalation.

questions.text: A production system logs API calls with latency, token usage, stop_reason, and tool calls. After a deployment, average latency triples with no change in token counts, and the stop_reason distribution shows a spike in tool_use stops. Which two are correct?
options: The new deployment introduced a tool or prompt change that causes the model to invoke tools more frequently, adding round-trip latency for each tool execution cycle — the latency increase reflects tool-call loop time, not slower model inference.

The next diagnostic step is checking whether the deployment's tool-invocation change was intentional or a side effect — e.g., a prompt rewrite that unintentionally made the model reach for tools more often — since the stop_reason data shows what changed but not why.
The model version was silently downgraded, causing slower inference.
The logging system is misconfigured after the deployment and is inflating latency measurements artificially.

The deployment caused the model to invoke tools more frequently, adding round-trip latency, so the fix is to revert the deployment immediately without further diagnosis, since any change that increases tool-use frequency should be treated as a regression by default.
questions.explanation: The stop_reason spike toward tool_use with flat token counts points to more tool round-trips adding latency, and the natural next step is checking whether that frequency change was intentional or a side effect. The hardest trap is option E: it correctly identifies the root cause, but jumps straight to reverting without diagnosis — treating any tool-use increase as inherently a regression, when it could just as easily be an intentional, beneficial change.

questions.text: A team is designing a long-running document processing pipeline and must choose between two context management strategies. Strategy P: at the start of each new document section, explicitly summarize completed sections and drop their raw content from the context. Strategy Q: maintain a full rolling context and rely on the model's context window to hold all processed content. The pipeline must process 200 documents of variable length. Which statement best describes when Strategy Q becomes untenable?
options: Strategy Q becomes untenable as soon as the second document is loaded, because multi-document contexts always cause cross-document confusion.
Strategy Q becomes untenable only if the pipeline runs for more than 60 minutes, regardless of token count.
Strategy Q is always preferable because summarization (Strategy P) introduces information loss that compounds across 200 documents.

Strategy Q becomes untenable when cumulative content approaches the model's context window limit, causing either hard truncation or progressive lost-in-the-middle degradation — the exact breakpoint depends on document lengths and the model's context capacity.
questions.explanation: Strategy Q's viability is purely a function of cumulative token count against the context window — it works fine while total content stays small, but as documents accumulate it eventually hits either hard truncation or progressive lost-in-the-middle degradation, and where that breakpoint falls depends on document lengths and the model's window size, not on a fixed document count or elapsed time. The trap is option C, declaring Q always inferior because summarization loss compounds across 200 documents — summarization loss (Strategy P) is real, but it's manageable and controllable, whereas rolling-context degradation under Q at scale is worse and effectively unrecoverable mid-session; 'summarization has some loss' doesn't make it worse than the alternative's failure mode, it makes it the safer tradeoff at scale.

questions.text: An agentic system for competitive intelligence runs a multi-step research loop: search → read → synthesize → search again. After 15 iterations, the system prompt occupies 8% of the context window, the accumulated search results occupy 78%, and the synthesis history occupies 12%. The team wants to maintain research quality for 30 more iterations. What is the correct compaction strategy?
options: Compact the system prompt first, since it is static content that doesn't need to remain in full.
Compact the accumulated search results: retain the synthesis history and key findings, drop raw search result content that has already been incorporated into the synthesis.
Compact the synthesis history, since it is the largest accumulated body of content and the model can regenerate it from the search results if needed.
No compaction is needed — the system prompt and synthesis history together are only 20%, leaving 80% headroom including the search results.
questions.explanation: Raw search results that have already been folded into the synthesis are the highest-value compaction target: dropping them recovers the most context (78%) while the synthesis history — the actual product of the work — stays intact and the reasoning trail is preserved. The trap is option C, compacting the synthesis history instead because it's large and 'the model can regenerate it from the search results if needed' — this treats the most valuable, hardest-to-reproduce content as disposable; regenerating synthesis would require re-processing the very search results this option assumes are still available, so compacting synthesis first doesn't actually save anything and risks losing conclusions that took 15 iterations to reach.

questions.text: A reliability engineer is reviewing an agentic pipeline that occasionally produces incomplete outputs — the model stops mid-task with stop_reason: end_turn before the task is done. The engineer hypothesizes three possible causes: (1) the model genuinely thinks it is done; (2) the model is running out of output token budget (max_tokens too low); (3) context window saturation is causing the model to lose track of remaining subtasks. What observability data would definitively distinguish between causes 2 and 3?
options: Check whether the outputs are always cut off at exactly the same character count — if so, it is cause 2.

Compare the usage.output_tokens value in the API response against the configured max_tokens limit. If output_tokens equals max_tokens, the model hit the output limit (cause 2). If output_tokens is well below max_tokens, the issue is not output truncation — investigate context size and task tracking.
Ask the model to explain why it stopped — its self-report will accurately distinguish between the three causes.
Increase max_tokens to the maximum supported value and observe whether the outputs complete — if they do, it was cause 2; if not, it was cause 3.
questions.explanation: Comparing usage.output_tokens against the configured max_tokens is a direct, mechanical test: equal means the response was genuinely cut off by the output budget (cause 2), while well-below means the model believed it was done and the real issue is elsewhere (context size or task tracking, cause 3). The trap is option D, raising max_tokens to the maximum and observing whether outputs complete — this is a real experiment, but it's destructive (it changes the running configuration) and less precise than just reading metadata that's already available in every response; it also conflates 'completing when given more room' with proving cause 2 specifically, when a context-tracking failure (cause 3) could also incidentally produce longer output without truly fixing task tracking.

questions.text: A contract analysis agent's 12,000-token system prompt (including the full contract) is identical across turns, but prompt cache hit rates are consistently 0%. Which two are correct?
options: The cache_control breakpoints are missing on the cacheable portions of the prompt — without explicit breakpoints marking where the stable prefix ends, the API does not know which content to cache.
The fix is placing the cache_control marker specifically after the stable system-prompt-and-contract content and before anything that varies per turn, not simply anywhere in the request.
The contract content embedded in the system prompt changes between sessions, but within a session the system prompt is static — caching should work regardless of breakpoints.
Prompt caching is disabled by default and must be explicitly enabled per API key in account settings.

The cache_control breakpoints are missing, so the fix is to add the marker on the first user message block instead of the system prompt block, since that's where the actual conversation with the model begins.
questions.explanation: Missing breakpoints explain the 0% hit rate, and the fix is placing the marker at the actual end of the stable prefix, not just anywhere. The hardest trap is option E: it correctly identifies missing breakpoints as the cause, but proposes marking the wrong content block — the repeated, stable content here is the system prompt with the embedded contract, not the user's first message, so marking that block wouldn't cache the prefix that's actually being repeated.

questions.text: An agent is asked to understand how authentication works across a legacy codebase with no documentation. The task requires finding every place a session token is validated, which spans middleware, three microservices, and a shared library. A developer suggests having the main agent read every file in the repository up front to build complete context before answering. What is the better approach and why?
options: Reading every file up front is correct — without full context, the agent cannot be certain it found every validation site.

Spawn a subagent to investigate a specific, narrow question (e.g., 'find all functions that validate a session token') and have it return a structured summary, while the main agent preserves high-level coordination instead of accumulating every file's full content in its own context.
Use only Grep across the entire repository in a single call and treat the raw match list as the final answer, since Grep is exhaustive by construction.
Increase max_tokens on the main agent's calls so it has enough room to read every file without truncation.
questions.explanation: Delegating the narrow investigation to a subagent isolates the verbose exploration — reading many files, tracing call chains through middleware, services, and the shared library — into a separate context, so the main agent gets back a compact structured summary instead of accumulating every file's raw content itself. The trap is option A, reading everything upfront to be 'certain' of completeness — this sounds like the thorough, safe choice, but it doesn't actually guarantee completeness either, while burning context on irrelevant files and setting up exactly the kind of context bloat that causes lost-in-the-middle degradation later in the same session.

questions.text: A team is investigating a bug in a large monorepo. After roughly two hours of continuous exploration in one long session, the agent begins giving answers that reference "typical patterns" in the codebase instead of the specific classes it examined earlier in that same session — even though the earlier findings are technically still present in the conversation history. What technique most directly counteracts this degradation for the remainder of the investigation?
options: Switch the model to a larger context window model mid-session, since the root cause is running out of space, not degraded attention.

Have the agent maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings as it discovers them, and explicitly reference that file for subsequent questions instead of relying on the conversation history alone.
Increase the temperature parameter so the model produces more specific, less generic-sounding answers.
Restart the session from scratch with no prior context, since a two-hour session has exceeded a hard usable-context limit.
questions.explanation: A scratchpad file persists key findings outside the flow of conversation tokens, and explicitly pointing the agent back to it gives a reliable anchor to specific facts instead of depending on attention holding up over two hours of accumulated exploration. The trap is option A, switching to a larger context window model mid-session — the content is technically still present in context (nothing was truncated), so a bigger window doesn't fix an attention-degradation problem; it only delays the point where the same degradation would eventually recur, since it doesn't change how the model attends to buried content.

questions.text: An invoice-extraction pipeline reports 97% overall field-level accuracy and the team is considering removing human review entirely for extractions above a 0.9 confidence score. Before doing so, a data scientist insists on running stratified sampling across document type and field before finalizing this decision. What risk does this stratified sampling step specifically catch that the aggregate 97% figure could hide?
options: It verifies that the extraction tool's JSON schema has no syntax errors, which the aggregate accuracy figure cannot detect on its own.
It reveals whether the 97% average is masking a much lower accuracy on a minority document type or a specific field, which a simple random sample might under-represent given its low volume.
It measures the API's response latency across different document sizes, which is unrelated to extraction correctness but often correlates with it.
It confirms that the Message Batches API is processing all 100 documents within the 24-hour window, which the accuracy metric does not track.
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling deliberately guarantees enough samples from every document type and field — including low-volume ones a simple random sample would barely touch — so it can catch a minority segment performing far worse than the 97% aggregate suggests, which is exactly the risk of trusting a single blended accuracy number before removing human review. The trap is option C, latency across document sizes 'often correlates with' accuracy — this smuggles in a plausible-sounding but irrelevant metric; latency measures processing time, not correctness, and stratified sampling for a confidence-threshold decision has nothing to do with response speed.

questions.text: A calibration exercise finds that when the extraction model reports 0.9 confidence, the actual empirical accuracy in that confidence bucket—measured against a labeled validation set—is only 68%. The team currently auto-approves everything at or above 0.9 confidence with no human review. What does this finding imply, and what is the correct response?
options: The model's confidence score is systematically overconfident at that bucket; the auto-approval threshold must be raised, or that bucket routed to human review, based on the calibrated empirical accuracy rather than the model's raw reported score.
The 0.9 confidence score is fine as reported; a 68% empirical accuracy is expected variance and does not require any threshold adjustment.
The validation set itself must be mislabeled, since a well-trained model's confidence score should always match empirical accuracy by definition.
The extraction schema should be changed to remove confidence scoring entirely, since it has been shown to be unreliable in this case.
questions.explanation: A 22-point gap between reported confidence (0.9) and empirical accuracy (68%) in that bucket is systematic overconfidence, and the fix is exactly what calibration is for: adjust the operational threshold — or route that bucket to human review — based on the measured empirical accuracy rather than trusting the model's raw self-reported score. The trap is option C, blaming the validation set for being mislabeled — this inverts the entire logic of calibration, which exists precisely because a model's confidence isn't guaranteed to match reality until independently validated; treating the validation set as the thing that must be wrong assumes the conclusion calibration is designed to test.

questions.text: A synthesis subagent combines findings from a web-search subagent and a document-analysis subagent into a final research report. The web source states a metric was "5.2% as of January" and the document source states "4.8% as of June" for what appears to be the same metric. The synthesis subagent's output schema does not currently include a date field per claim, only the claim text and a source name. What is the risk of this schema gap, and what is the fix?
options: The risk is minor — synthesis quality is unaffected by missing dates as long as both source names are correctly attributed to each claim.

Without a per-claim date field, the synthesis agent cannot distinguish a normal metric change over time from a genuine contradiction between sources, and may incorrectly flag this as a conflict between disagreeing sources; the fix is requiring a published/collected date field in each claim's structured output.
The risk is that the report will be too verbose; the fix is to drop the source name field instead, since the claim text alone is sufficient for synthesis.
The risk only affects citation formatting, not the correctness of the reported metric; the fix is a cosmetic change to how dates are displayed in the final report, not a schema change.
questions.explanation: Without a per-claim date, the synthesis agent can't tell a normal metric change over time (5.2% in January vs. 4.8% in June) from a genuine contradiction between two sources describing the same moment, so it risks flagging a non-conflict as a real disagreement — the fix is requiring a published/collected date field per claim. The trap is option D, calling this purely a display/formatting issue — it minimizes the actual damage: this isn't about how a date is rendered on the page, it's about the synthesis agent's classification logic itself lacking the input it needs to reason correctly about whether something is actually contested.

questions.text: Two credible sources report different Q2 growth figures for the same industry: a government report says 2.1%, a private industry dataset says 3.4%, both published within the same week. The synthesis agent's system prompt says: "When sources conflict, average the values to produce a single unified figure." What is the problem with this instruction, and what should replace it?
options: There is no problem — averaging is the standard, correct way to reconcile any two numeric values from different sources.

Averaging silently manufactures a number (2.75%) that neither source actually reported, hiding the real disagreement from the report's reader; the correct approach is to report both values with their sources explicitly, annotated as contested, and let the reader or a higher-context reviewer judge the discrepancy.
The problem is only that 2.75% should be rounded to one decimal place for presentation consistency; the averaging logic itself is sound.
The instruction is correct for numeric metrics but should be replaced with 'always prefer the government source' for non-numeric claims instead.
questions.explanation: Averaging the two figures manufactures a number (2.75%) that neither source reported, replacing a real disagreement with false precision — the correct approach is preserving both values with attribution, flagging them as contested, and letting a human or higher-context reviewer interpret the discrepancy. The trap is option D, replacing averaging with 'always prefer the government source' for non-numeric claims — this sounds like a principled tie-breaker, but silently picking a winner has the same core transparency problem as averaging: it hides the disagreement from the reader instead of surfacing it, just via a different mechanism.

questions.text: A multi-agent codebase migration runs for several hours across many subagents. Partway through, the process crashes due to an infrastructure issue. The team wants to resume without re-running completed work or losing track of what each agent had already found. What state persistence design supports this kind of crash recovery?
options: Each agent exports its state to a known location as it completes work, and the coordinator loads a manifest referencing those exports when resuming, injecting the relevant state into each agent's prompt.
Rely on the conversation history stored by the API provider to reconstruct all prior tool calls automatically after a crash.
Restart the entire migration from scratch, since partial agent state cannot be reliably persisted outside a single session.
Have each subagent write its full reasoning trace to a shared log file that the coordinator re-reads as raw text on resume.
questions.explanation: Structured state exports at each completion point, referenced by a manifest the coordinator loads on resume, let the system know exactly what's done and inject only the relevant state back into each agent's prompt — avoiding both redundant work and losing track of prior progress. The trap is option D, having each subagent write a full raw reasoning trace to a shared log for the coordinator to re-read as text — this sounds like it preserves everything, but unstructured raw logs give the coordinator no way to distinguish completed from in-progress work, and re-reading full reasoning traces reintroduces the exact context-bloat problem that structured, summarized exports are meant to avoid.

questions.text: After a crash, the coordinator resumes a multi-agent codebase exploration using saved manifests. One subagent's exported state references analysis of a file that a teammate has since modified. What should the coordinator do?
options: Inform the resuming agent about the specific file change so it can perform targeted re-analysis of just that file, rather than treating the entire prior exploration as stale.
Discard the entire manifest and restart the full exploration from zero, since any file change invalidates all prior findings.
Ignore the file change and proceed with the stale analysis, since re-analysis would cost additional tokens.
Pause the resume process indefinitely until every file in the codebase has been re-verified as unchanged.
questions.explanation: Targeted re-analysis of just the changed file lets the agent correct the one thing that's actually stale while reusing everything else from the manifest that's still valid — this is the entire point of persisting structured state, rather than treating any single change as grounds to discard it all. The trap is option B, discarding the entire manifest because 'any file change invalidates all prior findings' — this treats staleness as global when it's local; most of the exploration remains accurate, and throwing it all away to be safe wastes exactly the completed work the manifest was designed to preserve.

questions.text: A customer support agent's conversation history has grown to 40 turns. The agent recently forgot the exact refund amount ($847.32) mentioned in turn 6, instead referencing "the refund amount" vaguely in turn 38. Which two changes correctly address this?
options: Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers) into a persistent "case facts" block included in every prompt, separate from the summarized turn history.
Place key figures near the beginning or end of the aggregated context, since models reliably process information at the edges of long inputs but may drop details from the middle.
Increase max_tokens on the response so the model has more room to search back through all 40 turns for the figure.
Instruct the model to always re-read the entire 40-turn history verbatim before every response, rather than relying on any summarization.
Place the persistent case-facts block in the middle of the aggregated context, right where the summarized turn history sits, so it stays close to the most contextually relevant surrounding text.
questions.explanation: A persistent case-facts block keeps transactional numbers available regardless of summarization, and placing key figures near the start or end of the context mitigates the lost-in-the-middle effect. The hardest trap is option E: it borrows the right concept — proximity to relevant text — but applies it backwards; the middle of a long context is exactly the position models attend to least reliably, so deliberately placing the persistent facts there reintroduces the very failure mode ($847.32 fading by turn 38) the fix is meant to prevent.

questions.text: An order-lookup tool returns 40+ fields (shipping carrier metadata, warehouse codes, internal SKUs, etc.), but a return-processing agent only needs 5 of them (order ID, item, purchase date, return window, refund amount). Which two changes correctly manage context here?
options: Trim the tool's raw response to only the relevant fields before it's appended to the conversation, discarding the rest.

If some of the discarded fields might be needed for a distinct future task, retrieve them via a separate, targeted tool call only when that task actually requires them, rather than keeping them in context "just in case."
Keep all 40+ fields in every turn, since dropping any field risks losing information the model might need later.
Summarize all 40+ fields into a single vague sentence like "order details were retrieved" to save the most tokens possible.

Trim the tool response to only the relevant fields, but store the discarded 35+ fields in a separate untrimmed log file the agent can re-read in full whenever it needs any additional detail, rather than making a new targeted tool call.
questions.explanation: Trimming the tool response to the fields actually needed keeps context proportional to relevance, and fetching any discarded field later via a separate targeted call avoids paying for information speculatively. The hardest trap is option E: it keeps the correct trim, but the fallback undoes it — re-reading a full untrimmed log "whenever it needs any additional detail" reloads all 35+ discarded fields at once instead of the one or two actually needed, relocating the token cost rather than avoiding it.

questions.text: A customer says, mid-conversation, "I want to talk to a person." Separately, another customer's request falls into a genuine gap in policy — competitor price matching, which the written policy only addresses for the company's own site. Which two escalation behaviors are correct for these two cases?
options: Escalate the first customer to a human immediately, honoring the explicit request without first attempting further investigation or persuasion.
Escalate the second customer because the policy is silent on their specific situation, not because the request is inherently too complex to reason about.
Continue attempting to resolve the first customer's issue for a few more turns, since a request for a human doesn't by itself justify immediate escalation.
Resolve the second customer's request by applying the closest analogous policy rule automatically, without surfacing the gap to a human.

Escalate the first customer to a human only after confirming their negative sentiment score crosses a numeric threshold, since an explicit verbal request alone isn't sufficient signal to act on immediately.
questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human should be honored immediately without further persuasion attempts, and a genuine policy gap is exactly the trigger the escalation path exists for. The hardest trap is option E: requiring a sentiment threshold sounds like due diligence before escalating, but the customer already gave the clearest possible signal by asking directly — gating that on a separate, less reliable sentiment score (the exact heuristic shown to fail in the companion question) adds a barrier the explicit request doesn't need.

questions.text: An escalation system currently escalates automatically whenever sentiment analysis detects strong negative language, and also whenever the model's self-reported confidence score is below 6/10. Both heuristics perform poorly in practice. Which two statements correctly explain why?
options: Sentiment doesn't reliably correlate with actual case complexity — a frustrated customer can have a simple request, and a calm customer can have a genuinely complex one.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, especially on hard cases where the model is often confidently wrong rather than appropriately uncertain.
Both heuristics are fundamentally sound and simply need their thresholds tuned to more extreme values until performance improves.
Both heuristics are individually unreliable, but combining sentiment and self-reported confidence into a single weighted score corrects for each one's weaknesses.
Self-reported confidence is unreliable specifically because the 0-10 scale is too coarse; switching to a continuous 0-100 scale would resolve the calibration problem.
questions.explanation: Sentiment tone doesn't track case complexity, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated especially on hard cases where the model is often confidently wrong rather than appropriately uncertain. The hardest trap is option E: it sounds like a plausible engineering fix, but the problem isn't granularity — a model that's confidently wrong on a 0-10 scale would be just as confidently wrong on a 0-100 scale; finer resolution doesn't touch the actual calibration defect underneath the number.

questions.text: A search subagent's tool call fails. The team is deciding how to report this to the coordinator. Which two of the following are consistent with sound error propagation design?
options: Return structured error context including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results already gathered, and possible alternative approaches.
Distinguish clearly between an access failure (e.g., a timeout, which may warrant a retry decision) and a valid empty result (a successful query that simply found nothing).
Return a generic status like "search unavailable" for every failure type, to keep the coordinator's error-handling logic simple.
Silently return an empty result marked as successful, so the overall workflow doesn't need to handle a partial-failure case.

Return structured error context, but omit the possible alternative approaches field, since suggesting alternatives is the coordinator's job to decide, not something the subagent reporting the failure should include.
questions.explanation: Returning structured error context gives the coordinator what it needs to make an intelligent recovery decision, and distinguishing an access failure from a valid empty result prevents misreading one as the other. The hardest trap is option E: "deciding is the coordinator's job" is true, but it conflates deciding with being informed — the subagent surfacing possible alternative approaches doesn't make the decision for the coordinator, it just gives the coordinator more to decide with, which is exactly what sound error propagation is for.

questions.text: During a long codebase-exploration session, the agent starts giving inconsistent answers and referencing "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it identified earlier in the same session. Which two changes correctly address this context degradation?
options: Maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings as they're discovered, and reference it explicitly for subsequent questions instead of relying on the model recalling details from much earlier in the same long session.

Delegate verbose exploration sub-questions (e.g., "find all test files," "trace this dependency chain") to subagents, so the main session preserves high-level coordination without accumulating all the exploratory noise itself.
Continue in the same session and simply ask the model to "try harder to remember" the specific classes discovered earlier.
Restart with a completely empty context and no summary at all, so the model isn't influenced by any potentially stale prior findings.

Maintain a scratchpad file, but have the model regenerate it from scratch at the start of every new question in the session instead of appending to it incrementally, to guarantee it always reflects the latest understanding.
questions.explanation: A scratchpad file persists key findings outside the model's in-context recall, and delegating verbose exploratory sub-questions to subagents keeps that noise out of the main session. The hardest trap is option E: it keeps the correct tool (a scratchpad file) but regenerating it from scratch each time relies on the same in-session recall that's already degrading to reconstruct it — instead of a persistent record immune to context drift, it becomes just another thing the model has to remember correctly under the same failing conditions.

questions.text: After adopting stratified sampling by document type, a team looks at the smallest stratum — handwritten invoices, only 40 records out of 50,000 total. They draw 2 samples from that stratum, find both correctly extracted, and conclude the stratum is now safe to automate with no human review. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: The conclusion is valid — stratified sampling already accounts for stratum size proportionally, so drawing any number of samples from each stratum is sufficient by design.

Two samples is far too small to estimate that stratum's error rate with any real confidence; for a stratum this small, the sample size needed for a meaningful estimate may approach reviewing the entire 40-record stratum rather than a token draw.

The conclusion is invalid, but only because stratified sampling should never be applied to a stratum smaller than 1% of the total population; a stratum that small should be merged into the next-largest stratum instead.
The conclusion is invalid because handwritten invoices should be excluded from the automated pipeline entirely, regardless of what any sample shows.
questions.explanation: Stratification guarantees that every stratum gets represented in the sample, but it says nothing about whether the number drawn from a given stratum is large enough to estimate that stratum's error rate reliably — two samples from a 40-record stratum could show 2/2 correct by chance even if the stratum's true error rate is high. The trap is option C, inventing a specific-sounding '1% of total population' threshold rule for when to merge strata — it has the shape of a real statistical convention, but no such rule exists here; the actual fix is sizing the sample (or reviewing the stratum in full, given how small it is) to the confidence the decision requires, not discarding the stratum's own visibility.

questions.text: A synthesis agent processes two filings from the same company: an April earnings report stating Q1 revenue of $12M, and a July restated filing stating, explicitly, "This restatement corrects and supersedes the Q1 figure reported in April; the corrected Q1 revenue is $10.5M due to a revenue-recognition error." The agent's synthesis logic treats every numeric mismatch between sources as a contested figure to preserve with both values and attribution, per the standard rule against silently resolving conflicts. Applying that rule here, what is the correct outcome?
options: Preserve both $12M and $10.5M as contested figures with source attribution for each, exactly like any other numeric disagreement between two sources.

Recognize that this is not a genuine conflict between two independent sources but an explicit self-correction: the restated $10.5M is the current authoritative figure, and the April figure should be represented as the superseded prior value, not as a competing claim.
Average $12M and $10.5M into a blended $11.25M figure, since both numbers originate from the same company and should be reconciled into one number.
Discard the April figure entirely and omit any mention that a restatement occurred, since only the most recent number should ever appear in a synthesis report.
questions.explanation: The July filing isn't a second, independent source disagreeing with the first — it's the same source explicitly stating the earlier number is superseded, which makes this a correction to represent, not a conflict to preserve. The trap is option A: it correctly recalls the rule from other cases (never silently resolve a numeric disagreement, always preserve both with attribution), but applies it past where it holds — a source's own explicit self-correction isn't a disagreement between two claims, so treating it as one misrepresents a routine restatement as an open dispute.
